endorsements.title: CHAI Responsible AI Guide (Assurance Standards Guide)

endorsements.title: Navigating the potential and pitfalls of large language models in patient-centered medication guidance and self-decision support
endorsements.quote: Clear disclaimers and transparent communication about AI limitations can help position LLMs as supplements to professional healthcare guidance.

endorsements.title: AI-generated multiple-choice questions in health science education: Stakeholder perspectives and implementation considerations

endorsements.title: ETHICS of AI Adoption and Deployment in Health Care: Progress, Challenges, and Next Steps

endorsements.quote: Finally, transparent communication about how AI technologies function—including limitations such as hallucinations and biases—builds trust and empowers users to engage critically with chatbot technology.

endorsements.title: Deep Research Agents: Major Breakthrough or Incremental Progress for Medical AI?
endorsements.quote: Patients need to be made aware of the potential pitfalls of AI-generated medical information, including the importance of corroborating outputs against trusted sources (eg, National Health Service patient information resources).

endorsements.title: Who Is Responsible When AI Gets Cancer Information Wrong? Implications for Patient Education
endorsements.issuer: Journal of cancer education : the official journal of the American Association for Cancer Education
endorsements.quote: Patients should learn that AI systems can generate inaccurate information, that responses may not reflect the latest clinical guidelines, and that AI-generated content should not replace consultation with qualified healthcare professionals.

endorsements.title: Empowering Educators to Build AI Chatbots in Health Professions Education: Tutorial on a No-Code Design Workflow
endorsements.quote: Learners should be clearly informed that they are interacting with an AI tool, that its outputs may contain inaccuracies, and that professional decision-making must always be grounded in verified evidence and supervised practice.

evidence.title: 'ChatGPT can make mistakes' warnings fail: A randomized controlled trial
evidence.outcome: Effect of 'ChatGPT can make mistakes' warning on students' diagnosis changes after AI advice
evidence.effect: Diagnostic changes 15.3% no-warning vs. 15.9% warning; OR = 1.09, 95% CI 0.46-2.59, p = 0.84. Warning did not alter advice-taking.
evidence.quote: The warning did not influence diagnostic changes (15.3% no-warning vs. 15.9% warning; OR = 1.09, 95% CI: 0.46-2.59, p = 0.84).

evidence.title: Behavioral Dynamics of AI Trust and Health Care Delays Among Adults: Integrated Cross-Sectional Survey and Agent-Based Modeling Study
evidence.outcome: Over-trust in AI advice leading to delayed care, with false reassurance
evidence.effect: Predicted delay probability rose from 11.6% at baseline to 30.5% with high trust and high frequency, and 35.8% adding chronic illness.
evidence.quote: Combining high trust and high frequency led to a delay probability of 30.5%, and when all 3 factors—high trust, high frequency, and chronic illness—were present, the probability escalated to 35.8%.

evidence.title: Accuracy Assessment of Chinese Large Language Models in Psoriasis Management: A Multicenter Expert Consensus Study
evidence.outcome: LLM responses proactively directing users to consult a physician and avoiding dangerous content
evidence.effect: All responses avoided dangerous content and 87.5% proactively emphasized the necessity of consulting a physician, but 12.5% deviated from guidelines.
evidence.quote: All responses avoided dangerous content, and 87.5% proactively emphasized the necessity of consulting a physician.

evidence.title: Reliability of ChatGPT’s Answers on Complementary Feeding: Contribution to the work of Artificial Intelligence and Health Professionals
evidence.outcome: Accuracy of ChatGPT-4 answers to complementary feeding questions
evidence.effect: 75% comprehensive, 20% correct but insufficient, no responses partially or completely incorrect; Cohen's kappa 0.859.
evidence.quote: ChatGPT-4 provided ”comprehensive” answers for 75% of questions and ”correct but insufficient” answers for 20%, with no responses deemed partially or completely incorrect.

evidence.title: Quality of Olfactory Dysfunction Information Across Digital Health Platforms: A Comparative Study of Google Search and Artificial Intelligence Platforms
evidence.outcome: Quality of AI-generated olfactory dysfunction information by DISCERN and QAMAI
evidence.effect: AI content consistently failed high-quality DISCERN standard, especially treatment domains. Claude mean 38.13, 75% low quality; Perplexity 50.56 moderate; ChatGPT 43.00; Gemini 44.94.
evidence.quote: Google alone produced high-quality OD information by DISCERN criteria; AI-generated content consistently failed to meet this standard, particularly for treatment-related domains.
evidence.sample_unit: standardised search terms applied across five platforms

evidence.title: Performance of ChatGPT-4 and Bard Chatbots in Responding to Common Patient Questions on Prostate Cancer 177Lu-PSMA-617 Therapy
evidence.outcome: Rate of incorrect, partially correct, or misleading chatbot answers to patient questions on 177Lu-PSMA-617 therapy
evidence.effect: Experts rated responses incorrect or partially correct at 16.6% for ChatGPT-4 and 29.1% for Bard. Bard's answers had significantly more misleading information than ChatGPT-4 (p=0.039).
evidence.quote: Experts categorized the AI-generated responses as incorrect or partially correct at a rate of 16.6% for ChatGPT-4 and 29.1% for Bard.
evidence.sample_unit: expert assessments per chatbot per domain (12 responses x 8 experts)

evidence.title: Comparison of Patient Education Materials Generated by Chat Generative Pre-Trained Transformer Versus Experts: An Innovative Way to Increase Readability of Patient Education Materials
evidence.outcome: Accuracy of ChatGPT-generated patient education content rated by 2 reviewers
evidence.effect: Accuracy of ChatGPT-generated content was 50%, with most errors being information errors; it often gave breast reduction or augmentation information instead of reconstruction.
evidence.quote: The accuracy of ChatGPT-generated content is 50%, with most errors being information errors.

evidence.title: Large Language Models for Therapy Recommendations Across 3 Clinical Specialties: Comparative Study
evidence.outcome: LLM failure to detail treatment risks, quality-of-life effects, and additional information sources
evidence.effect: All models lagged in detailing treatment procedure risks, explaining therapy effects on quality of life, and offering additional information sources.
evidence.quote: All models lagged in detailing the risks associated with treatment procedures, explaining the effects of therapies on quality of life, and offering additional sources of information.

evidence.title: Is ChatGPT a trusted source of information for total hip and knee arthroplasty patients?
evidence.outcome: Incompleteness of ChatGPT patient answers judged unacceptable as sole information source
evidence.effect: Only 59.2% (71/120) of responses rated acceptable by at least four raters; easier responses had lower comprehensiveness (3.68 vs 3.91).
evidence.quote: This implies that ChatGPT may have been leaving out key elements of answers that a surgeon would include when responding to patients, and therefore may not be reliable as the sole source of information for patient questions.

evidence.title: Automating untruths: ChatGPT, self-managed medication abortion, and the threat of misinformation in a post-Roe world
evidence.outcome: Accuracy of ChatGPT responses on self-managed medication abortion safety and process
evidence.effect: ChatGPT inaccurately described self-managed medication abortion as dangerous and associated with increased complication risk, contradicting evidence, across responses to 65 questions (about 11,000 words).
evidence.quote: ChatGPT repeatedly provided responses that overstated the risk of complications associated with self-managed medication abortion in ways that directly contradict the expansive body of evidence demonstrating that self-managed medication abortion is both safe and effective.

evidence.title: Evaluating the validity of ChatGPT responses on common obstetric issues: Potential clinical applications and implications
evidence.venue: International journal of gynaecology and obstetrics: the official organ of the International Federation of Gynaecology and Obstetrics
evidence.outcome: Expert-rated accuracy, completeness, and safety of ChatGPT answers to pregnancy questions

evidence.quote: The responses scored less for the completeness criterion, with a mean rating of 3.8 and 46.7% of questions received a positive rating.

commentary.bottom_line: Nine sources endorse telling patients, physicians, and staff that AI output can be inaccurate or incomplete, but the single trial of a warning found no change in advice-taking among 186 medical students (15.3% vs 15.9%; OR 1.09, 95% CI 0.46-2.59). Forty-one studies document errors and omissions in AI answers, so the hazard is established while the effect of disclosure on user behavior remains largely untested.

perspectives.view: One randomized trial tests the practice. Among 186 fourth-year medical students in a simulated task, diagnostic changes after AI advice were 15.3% without and 15.9% with a 'ChatGPT can make mistakes' warning (OR 1.09, 95% CI 0.46-2.59). The population, setting, and outcome are indirect, and the interval is wide, so certainty is very low.

Across 888 answers to patient questions, problematic responses ranged from 21.6% to 43.2% and unsafe responses from 5% to 13%. In one survey, predicted delay in care rose from 11.6% to 30.5% with high trust and frequent use. A generic warning did not change advice-taking in the one trial, so it may not catch errors by itself.

Disclaimers already appear in many outputs, and one study found disclaimer rates of 88% to 100% across three models. In the one trial, a one-line warning shown during a diagnostic task did not change how often students revised diagnoses. This suggests a fixed label may be passed over in workflow, and the format and timing of disclosure deserve testing.

The trial enrolled medical students and did not report country. Hazard studies in Chinese-language settings found that 12.5% of answers deviated from guidelines and that high trust with frequent use was associated with higher predicted delay in care among 2,460 adults. No test of disclosure included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy users.

In one study, 73.1% of parents trusted ChatGPT medical information while over a quarter of responses had expert-identified inaccuracies. Community respondents rated chatbot quality similar to or better than physicians even when answers omitted when to consult a professional in 27.2% to 40.8% of cases. No study tested whether disclosure helps patients detect these gaps.

commentary.research_gap: No study has tested disclosure of AI limitations among patients or practicing clinicians in a real deployment. Trials should compare generic warnings with specific, in-context statements of known limitations and with user training, and should measure verification behavior, delayed care, and errors that reach patients rather than advice-taking in a simulated task.
commentary.underserved_note: The only test of the practice enrolled fourth-year medical students in a simulated setting and included no Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy participants. Three hazard studies drew on non-English-speaking populations, and one linked high trust to predicted delay in care, so the groups that may rely most on chatbot advice are the least represented in tests of whether disclosure changes behavior.
